newsitem.title: CANADA: NOVA CEO SEES MAJOR GASANDES EXPANSION.
newsitem.headline: NOVA CEO SEES MAJOR GASANDES EXPANSION.

text.p: The GasAndes pipeline to Chile from Argentina, officially opened on Thursday, will probably be expanded over the next decade far more than previously envisaged, NOVA Corp Chief Executive Ted Newall said.
"One of the facets of the gas pipeline business is that when you open up a new pipeline a lot of demand emerges that nobody anticipated," Newall told reporters by telephone from Mendoza, Argentina.
"Over the next 10 years, we're on our way to 700 (million cubic feet of gas) a day, but I'll be awfully surprised if we don't double that," he said.
Newall made his comments following the GasAndes opening ceremony attended by Argentine President Carlos Menem and Chilean President Eduardo Frei.
NOVA is operator of the 463 km (288 mile) pipeline that extends over the Andes Mountains to Santiago from Mendoza. It has a 56.5 percent interest in GasAndes.

NOVA's partners in the US$325 million project include Chilean power generation company Chilgener SA with 15 percent, Santiago gas distribution company Metrogas SA with 15 percent and Argentina's Compania General de Combustibles with 13.5 percent.
NOVA also has a 10 percent stake in the pipeline's accompanying Santiago gas distribution company and 15 percent of the first of three gas-fired power plants that will be fed by GasAndes supply.
The total project was valued at C$1.4 (US$1 billion), and NOVA's investment was pegged at C$300 million (US$219 million).

The pipeline, which took 22 months to build through harsh, mountainous terrain and disputes with the residents of some towns, was expected to deliver 194 million cubic feet of gas a day this year, 212 million in 2000 and 600 million in 2007.
Newall said the project would be a major force in reducing Santigo's severe smog problems by displacing existing fossil-fuel power generation.

"The customers asked GasAndes to build the pipeline because the big users of gas are three new power plants and those power plants are having to compete with coal-fired power and high sulphur residual oil-fired power and they needed to have very low-cost transportation," he said.
Newall said the group's next major challenge was to convince the Chilean government to convert Santiago's taxi, bus and truck fleets to natural gas from diesel fuel and gasoline.
He said NOVA's experience in building pipelines in Canada's Rocky Mountain region gave it the knowhow to construct GasAndes, which wrapped over elevations as high as 12,000 feet.
That made the design 50 percent shorter than an earlier competing proposal that would have avoided the high Andean peaks, he said.

"To fly the pipeline in a helicopter is to come away really spectacularly impressed by these prairie boys we have building pipelines," Newall said. ((Jeffrey Jones, Reuters Calgary Bureau (403) 531-1624))
